item.title: Yamanashi Wine & Katsunuma: Japan's Birthplace of Wine — Guide
item.description: Yamanashi is the birthplace and heart of the Japanese wine industry, centred on the Katsunuma area near Kofu, where the mild climate and the native Koshu grape, a pale pink variety used to make crisp, delicate white wines, have supported winemaking since the 1870s. Today the region is home to dozens of wineries ranging from historic family operations to modern estates, many offering tastings, cellar tours and even hands-on blending experiences, set among vineyards that turn golden in autumn and often within walking or cycling distance of one another.

item.title: Yamanashi Wine Festival: Tasting the Harvest in Japan's Wine Country — Guide
item.description: Yamanashi’s wine festivals are held in autumn around the grape harvest, gathering local wineries together for open-air tasting events that let visitors sample dozens of regional wines in a single place, often for a set entry fee that includes a tasting glass. Centred on the Katsunuma and Kofu wine districts, these festivals celebrate the region’s identity as the birthplace of Japanese wine, combining tastings with food stalls, local produce and a festive harvest-season atmosphere among the golden vineyards.

item.title: Best Restaurants & Food in Yamanashi: Hoto Nabe, Koshu Wine & Local Gourmet
item.description: Yamanashi feeds visitors from the mountain down. The cuisine here is shaped by geography — a landlocked basin ringed by high peaks that historically isolated communities and pushed local cooks to make the most of what the mountains produced: river fish, wild vegetables, mountain mushrooms, and the grapes that grow on sun-facing slopes above the Kofu Basin. The result is a food culture that is deeply rooted in the seasons and centred on a handful of dishes and products unlike anything produced elsewhere in Japan.
